Course description

Vibrations and waves are everywhere. If you take any system and disturb it from a stable equilibrium, the resultant motion will be waves and vibrations. Think of a guitar string—pluck the string, and it vibrates. The sound waves generated make their way to our ears, and we hear the string’s sound. Our eyes see what’s happening because they receive the electromagnetic waves of the light reflected from the guitar string, so that we can recognize the beautiful sinusoidal waves on the string. In fact, without vibrations and waves, we could not recognize the universe around us at all!

The amazing thing is that we can describe many fascinating phenomena arising from very different physical systems with mathematics. This course will provide you with the concepts and mathematical tools necessary to understand and explain a broad range of vibrations and waves. You will learn that waves come from many interconnected (coupled) objects when they are vibrating together. We will discuss many of these phenomena, along with related topics, including mechanical vibrations and waves, sound waves, electromagnetic waves, optics, and gravitational waves.

Exercise:
TITLE: Practice Final Exam 1

8.03SC Physics III: Vibrations and Waves
Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Fall 2016
Practice Final Exam 1 (covers Lectures 1-23)


Problem 3.1 (16 pts)

The electric field for a TE mode in an infinitely long (in the x direction) perfectly conducting rectangular waveguide (a < b) is given by

    E⃗(x,y,z,t) = E₀ cos(k_y y + φ_y) cos(k_x x − ωt) ẑ

[Figure 1: A perfectly conducting waveguide — a rectangular box drawn in perspective with its long axis along x, extending indefinitely to the right (the open end is drawn with dotted lines and a wavy field pattern inside). The y-axis points up and the z-axis points toward the viewer, both from the origin at the near-left corner. The height of the box along y is labelled a, and the depth along z is labelled b, with a < b. The guide is infinitely long in the x direction.]

(a) Find k_y and φ_y that satisfy the boundary conditions.
(b) Write down the dispersion relation for this mode of the waveguide.
(c) What is the lowest frequency that will propagate in this mode?
(d) What is the magnetic field B⃗(x,y,z,t) associated with the electric field of this mode?


Problem 3.2 (16 pts)

The figure below shows a system of masses. The mass of 2m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant 2k, while the mass of m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant k. The masses are then coupled to each other with an elastic band of length L, under tension T = 2kL. The masses are constrained to move in the x direction only. At equilibrium the masses have the same x position and the springs are uncompressed. There is no friction or gravity. The displacements from equilibrium are small enough (x₁, x₂ ≪ L), so that the tension in the band stays constant.

[Figure 2: A system of coupled oscillators — two vertical walls, one on the left and one on the right, with the region between them drawn in a vertical plane. Axes at the upper left show y pointing up and x pointing right. Near the top of the gap sits a circular mass labelled m, connected by a coil spring of constant k running horizontally to the right-hand wall. Near the bottom sits a circular mass labelled 2m, connected by a coil spring of constant 2k running horizontally to the left-hand wall. The two masses are joined to each other by a vertical elastic band of length L under tension T = 2kL, drawn as a double-headed vertical arrow between them. Each mass carries a small horizontal arrow marking its displacement coordinate: x₂ for the upper mass m, x₁ for the lower mass 2m. Both masses move only in the x direction, so the coupling band tilts slightly when they are displaced.]

(a) Write down the coupled differential equations describing the displacement of the masses from equilibrium {x₁, x₂}.
(b) Find the normal mode frequencies of the system.
(c) On the two figures included on the next page sketch the normal modes of the system; be sure to clearly indicate both the magnitude and direction of the motion of the masses.


Problem 3.3 (16 pts)

(a) An optical fiber consists of a solid rod of material with index of refraction n_f surrounded by a cylindrical shell of material with index n_c. Find the largest angle θ so that a wave incident on the solid rod from air with index n_a remains in the solid rod (express your answer in terms of n_f, n_c, and n_a).

[Figure 3: An optical fiber — a horizontal three-layer slab drawn in cross section. The middle layer, the core, is labelled n_f. Above and below it are cladding layers, both labelled n_c. To the left of the fiber is air, labelled n_a. A ray arrives from the upper left and strikes the flat left end face of the core, making an angle θ with the horizontal fiber axis; θ is marked between the incoming ray and the axis at the entrance face.]

(b) Unpolarized light propagating in vacuum reflects off the surface of a liquid with index n. The reflected ray strikes a screen 25 cm away at a height of 20 cm and is observed to be 100% polarized. What is n?

(c) Consider a medium in which waves propagate with a dispersion relation

    ω² = ω₀² + A²k²

where ω is the wave (angular) frequency, k is the wave number, and ω₀ and A are real constants.

    (i) What is the range of frequencies ω for which waves can propagate?
    (ii) Compute v_phase and v_group. Make a carefully labeled sketch of each as a function of ω in the plots provided.

[Figure 4: Plot the phase/group velocity — two empty grid plots side by side, provided for the student's sketches. The left plot has vertical axis labelled V_p (phase velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω; the right plot has vertical axis labelled V_g (group velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω. Both are blank graph paper with no data drawn and no numerical scale.]


Problem 3.4 (16 pts)

A monochromatic beam is incident on N slits, which results in an intensity pattern as a function of angle on a screen some distance away as shown in the figure below. Each slit has a width D and the distance between the centers of the slits is d. The distance between the screen and the slits is very large.

[Figure 5: Interference pattern due to N slits — a plot of Intensity (vertical axis, no numerical scale) against sin θ (horizontal axis, no numerical scale). The pattern is symmetric about the center. A tall central principal maximum sits at the middle, flanked by principal maxima of decreasing height on each side: the first-order pair is somewhat shorter than the central one, the second-order pair shorter still, and a small third-order pair is visible farther out. The fourth-order principal maximum is absent — the pattern is flat where it would fall, because the first diffraction minimum suppresses it — and small low bumps resume beyond that point. Between each pair of adjacent principal maxima there are three small subsidiary bumps.]

From the pattern deduce the following:

(a) The number of slits N on which the beam is incident. Explain your reasoning.
(b) The ratio d/D. Explain your reasoning.
(c) Now suppose that the width of the slits is reduced to ~0, while the intensity of the monochromatic beam is increased so that the intensity of the central maximum is unchanged. On top of the plot (showing the original intensity pattern in dashed lines) provided, draw the resulting intensity pattern.

[Figure 6: Plot the resulting intensity pattern as D → 0 — an empty plot frame provided for the student's answer, with the original intensity pattern of Figure 5 reproduced in dashed lines underneath.]


Problem 3.5 (20 pts)

A string of length 2L with mass density µ is placed under tension T and is fixed at both ends. At time t = 0, the displacement of the string is zero everywhere but it is struck so that a transverse velocity is imparted to a section of the string. The initial conditions of the string are (a ≪ L):

    y(x, t = 0) = 0

    ẏ(x, t = 0) = v₀      for L − a ≤ x < L
                = −v₀     for L ≤ x < L + a
                = 0       elsewhere

[Figure 7: The initial transverse velocity of the string at time t = 0; the initial displacement is zero everywhere — a horizontal string stretched between two hatched walls, the left wall at x = 0 and the right wall at x = 2L, with the midpoint x = L marked; the distance from each wall to the midpoint is labelled L. The velocity profile is drawn as a pair of adjacent rectangular pulses straddling the midpoint. Just to the left of x = L a rectangle of width a rises above the string to a height labelled v₀. Immediately to the right of x = L a rectangle of the same width a drops below the string to a depth labelled v₀ (i.e. −v₀). The velocity is zero everywhere else along the string.]

(a) Using the plot (Figure 8) provided, sketch the first three normal modes of vibration for this string, regardless of whether or not they are excited.

[Figure 8: Plot the first three normal modes — three identical empty plots stacked vertically, labelled (1), (2), and (3). Each shows a straight horizontal string at rest spanning the gap between a left and a right hatched wall, provided for the student to draw the mode shapes on.]

(b) What is the amplitude of the n-th normal mode after the string is struck? What is the lowest unexcited mode?

(c) Sketch the displacement of the string at time t = (L/2)√(µ/T) in the plot provided.

[Figure 9: Plot the displacement of the string — a single empty plot showing the straight horizontal string at rest between the left and right hatched walls, provided for the student's sketch.]


Problem 3.6 (18 pts)

A charged particle of mass M and charge +Q is attached to the end of a spring of spring constant k. The spring lies along the x-axis and the equilibrium point is at the origin. The particle is displaced from equilibrium by a distance A in the x direction, and released at t = 0. Assume that the size of the particle is much smaller than A, so it can be treated as a point charge, and that the damping rate is very small.

[Figure 10: An oscillating charge — a vertical wall on the left with a horizontal coil spring of constant k attached to it, extending to the right. At the free end of the spring is a circular particle labelled Q,M. Axes are drawn above the spring: z points up and x points to the right, with the origin at the particle's equilibrium position. The particle oscillates along the x-axis.]

(a) Calculate the electric field radiated by the particle along an arbitrary direction in the x−z plane, at a distance R, where R ≫ A.
(b) Calculate the total time averaged power radiated by the particle.
(c) Assuming that the power radiated does not change appreciably as a function of time, give a simple rough estimate of the time it will take for the particle to decrease its amplitude of oscillation to 1/e of its initial value. Is this assumption realistic?
(d) A more refined estimate can be obtained using that dA/dt = (dA/dE) × (dE/dt), and using the average power radiated over a given cycle for dE/dt. Use this to calculate the time it will take the particle to decrease its oscillation amplitude to 1/e of its initial value.

Let's think about it strategically rather than me just picking for you: which topics do you feel *most* solid on right now? Like, if you had to rank waveguides, coupled oscillators, optics/polarization, N-slit diffraction, wave pulses on a string, and radiation from an accelerating charge — which one or two would you say "yeah, I've got the core idea of this"?

That'll tell us where to start, since starting where you're confident usually builds momentum for the harder ones.

exchanges.student: the Brewster one maybe, but I’m already lost on why the screen distances matter tbh.
exchanges.tutor:
Good instinct to question that — the 25 cm and 20 cm aren't just random numbers, they're telling you something *geometric* about the light ray's path.

Let's think about the setup. You've got:
- unpolarized light hitting the liquid surface,
- reflecting off at some angle,
- and traveling in a straight line until it hits a screen 25 cm away (that's the straight-line distance the ray travels),
- landing at a height of 20 cm on the screen.

So here's a question for you: if you think of the reflected ray as the hypotenuse of a right triangle, with the screen distance (25 cm) as one side and the height (20 cm) as another... what geometric quantity would let you find the *angle* of that ray?

And once you have that angle — what physical angle does it correspond to, if the problem says the reflected ray is 100% polarized?

exchanges.student: wait so is it like sin θ = 20/25? I’m not even sure if that θ is from the surface or the normal tbh.
exchanges.tutor:
You're on the right track with setting up a triangle from those two numbers — that part's good! But pause on which sides go where.

Think physically about the reflection geometry: the ray reflects off the horizontal liquid surface and travels through space to hit a vertical screen. If the screen is 25 cm *away* (horizontally, along the direction of travel) and the ray rises to a height of 20 cm by the time it gets there... which of those two distances is "how far along" the ray travels horizontally, and which is "how far up" it goes?

Once you sort that out: draw the right triangle with the reflected ray as the hypotenuse. The angle between the ray and the *horizontal surface* — is that the angle whose tangent (or sine, depending on setup) is (vertical)/(horizontal)? And how is that angle related to the angle measured *from the normal*, which is what Brewster's angle formula actually uses?

Try sketching it out — what do you get for tan of the angle from the surface, and then what's the complement?

exchanges.student: ugh now I’m mixing up like 3 angles lol. Can u just explain the whole Brewster setup from scratch real quick?
exchanges.tutor:
Totally fair — let's slow down and rebuild it piece by piece, no formulas yet, just the picture.

**Step 1: The surface and the normal.**
Picture the liquid surface as a flat horizontal line. At any point on that surface, the *normal* is the imaginary vertical line perpendicular to it (pointing straight up, away from the liquid).

**Step 2: Angle of incidence / reflection.**
A light ray comes down from above, hits the surface, and reflects. The **angle of incidence** and **angle of reflection** are both measured *from the normal* (that vertical line), not from the surface itself. Snell's law and Brewster's law both use this "from the normal" convention.

**Step 3: Brewster's angle.**
Brewster's angle is a special angle of incidence (measured from the normal!) at which the reflected light is 100% polarized. There's a simple relation between Brewster's angle and the index of refraction of the liquid — do you remember the general shape of that formula (even roughly), relating $\theta_B$ and $n$?

**Step 4: Now — geometry of the ray to the screen.**
The reflected ray leaves the surface at angle $\theta_B$ from the normal (i.e., from vertical). It travels in a straight line to a screen, covering some horizontal distance and rising some vertical height.

So here's the key question: if $\theta_B$ is measured from the **vertical**, and the ray moves 20 cm vertically while covering 25 cm... horizontally? or is 25 cm the straight-line hypotenuse? — think about what "distance away" and "height" most naturally mean for a screen setup, and which trig ratio (sin, cos, or tan) of $\theta_B$ that gives you.

Try writing that ratio out — what do you get?

This is a direct request for an explanation of how to approach/solve this part of the problem, which falls under explicitly asking about how to solve the problem and discussing concepts related to the material."}

exchanges.student: I vaguely remember tan θ_B = n maybe? but idk if 25 is horizontal or the actual ray length, that wording keeps messing me up fr.
exchanges.tutor:
Good, you're recalling the right relation — $\tan\theta_B = n$ (for light going from vacuum into the medium), so hang onto that.

Now for the geometry: think about what a "screen" physically is — it's a flat surface set up somewhere in the room to catch the light, and we're told the ray "strikes" it at a certain height. The "25 cm away" most naturally describes *how far the screen is positioned* from the point of reflection, i.e. the distance along the floor/table, not the length of the light ray's actual path through the air.

So if you set up a right triangle where:
- the vertical leg is the height where the ray hits the screen,
- the horizontal leg is how far away the screen is,

then the angle between the ray and the **normal** (vertical) is the angle whose **tangent** = (horizontal)/(vertical), since tangent = opposite/adjacent relative to that angle.

Try it: which side is opposite the angle-from-vertical, and which is adjacent? Once you identify that, what expression do you get for $\tan\theta_B$ in terms of 20 and 25 — and then, using the relation you just recalled, what's $n$?

This shows an attempt to recall a concept/formula and confusion about problem setup, but no definitive answer is given yet. exchanges.student: so then tan θ_B = 25/20 and n = 1.25? I’m not confident tho, like why isn’t it 20/25 if the ray goes upward.
exchanges.tutor:
You've got the right number and the right instinct to double check — let's nail down *why* it's 25/20 and not the flip, since that reasoning will save you on similar problems later.

Draw the right triangle again: the angle $\theta_B$ is measured from the **normal**, which is the *vertical* line. In a right triangle, "adjacent" and "opposite" are always relative to *which angle you're looking at*.

- The **vertical** leg (20 cm) — is that along the same direction as the normal, or perpendicular to it?
- The **horizontal** leg (25 cm) — is that along the surface, i.e. perpendicular to the normal?

Since $\theta_B$ is measured from the vertical (normal) direction, the leg *along* that vertical direction (20 cm) is the **adjacent** side to $\theta_B$, and the leg *perpendicular* to it (25 cm, horizontal) is the **opposite** side.

So $\tan\theta_B = \text{opposite}/\text{adjacent} = 25/20$ — matching what you got.

Does that match your picture now, or does it help to sketch the angle at the point where the ray leaves the surface and see which sides it's "between"?

However, they express uncertainty and ask a conceptual question about why the ratio isn't inverted, which is a request for clarification/discussion of the underlying geometry/concept rather than a new calculation request."}

exchanges.student: ok maybe, but now I’m spiraling on whether reflected ray angle = incident angle here or if Brewster changes that somehow.
exchanges.tutor:
Good question to pin down — the answer is **no, Brewster's angle doesn't break the law of reflection.**

Think about it this way: Brewster's angle is just a *special value* of the angle of incidence — nothing about the geometry of reflection changes. The law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal) always holds for any angle of incidence, whether or not it happens to be Brewster's angle.

What *is* special about Brewster's angle is a polarization fact: at that particular angle, the component of light polarized parallel to the plane of incidence doesn't reflect at all — only the perpendicular-polarization component reflects. That's why the reflected ray is 100% polarized only when the incidence angle equals $\theta_B$.

So in your triangle: the angle you computed **is** the angle of incidence (measured from the normal), and it's *also* the angle of reflection — they're the same angle, and that's the angle you plug into $\tan\theta_B = n$.

Does that resolve the worry, or is there a specific step where you thought Brewster's condition might change the reflected ray's direction?

This is a conceptual question about material covered in the problem, not a direct request for the answer, not a calculation request, and not yet a stated solution or error to evaluate."}

exchanges.student: yeah kinda, but now I feel like I only followed this one by vibes 😭 can we switch to the dispersion one, maybe that’s more formula-y?
exchanges.tutor:
Ha, fair enough — but for what it's worth, you *did* get Brewster's angle right by reasoning through the geometry, not just vibes. That's the real skill. 🙂

Let's switch to the dispersion relation problem then:

$$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + A^2k^2$$

**Part (i)** asks: for what range of $\omega$ can waves actually propagate?

Here's a way to think about it: $k$ is the wavenumber of a *real, physical* traveling wave. So $k$ should be some real number (it can't be imaginary — that would mean the wave dies out in space instead of oscillating).

So — try solving the dispersion relation for $k$ in terms of $\omega$. What do you get? And then ask yourself: for what values of $\omega$ is that expression for $k$ guaranteed to be real?

exchanges.student: I get k = sqrt(ω²-ω₀²)/A I think, so does that mean only ω > ω₀? Not sure if = counts.
exchanges.tutor:
You've got the right expression and the right idea — for $k$ to be real, you need the stuff under the square root to be non-negative, i.e. $\omega^2 \ge \omega_0^2$, which gives you $\omega \ge \omega_0$ (taking positive $\omega$).

Now think about the boundary case: if $\omega = \omega_0$ exactly, what does $k$ come out to be? And physically, does $k = 0$ correspond to an actual traveling wave (something with a wavelength, moving through space), or does it describe something else — like a wave that's frozen in space, oscillating in time everywhere at once?

That should tell you whether to include the equals sign or not.

grade.overview: The tutor demonstrates strong Socratic technique throughout: consistently asking guiding questions rather than giving answers, building on student progress (e.g., affirming the correct tan formula before probing the reasoning), and redirecting appropriately when the student wants to switch topics. The main weakness is response length — particularly in Turns 5 and 6, the tutor delivers multi-paragraph explanations with multiple embedded questions when the student was already confused, which risks overwhelming rather than scaffolding. No direct answer-giving, no rewriting of student work, and no off-topic drift were observed.
grade.judge_reasoning: Pedagogy (1.1–1.3) is strong: the tutor never gives submission-ready answers, consistently uses questions to guide reasoning, builds on student responses (e.g., 'Good, you're recalling the right relation'), and provides process-level feedback (e.g., explaining why tan = opposite/adjacent matters for future problems). Dialogue quality (2.1–2.2) is also strong: the tutor advances the conversation without spiraling, and appropriately redirects when the student wants to switch problems. The only clear deduction is in 3.1: Turns 5 and 6 are notably long and lecture-like, with multiple sub-steps and questions bundled together, which is mismatched to a student who explicitly said they were confused and mixing up angles — a shorter, more targeted prompt would have been more appropriate. Tone and formative framing (3.2) are consistently supportive and non-evaluative throughout.
